modules.content:
## A Traveler’s First Encounter: Ordering a Coffee in Cairo  

You step out of the bustling hotel lobby onto a sun‑lit street. A fragrant breeze carries the scent of freshly brewed Arabic coffee. A friendly vendor smiles and asks, “**قهوة؟**” (qahwa?). You want to reply, but the letters on the sign above the stall look like a secret code: **ق ه و ة**. How do those shapes translate into the sounds you just heard?  

The moment you can recognize and pronounce each of those letters, the door to everyday Arabic opens. This chapter equips you with the tools to read, write, and say every basic Arabic sound—exactly the skill set you need to navigate cafés, markets, and transport hubs across the Arab world.

---

## 1. The Arabic Alphabet at a Glance  

Arabic is written from **right to left** and consists of **28 consonantal letters**. Unlike English, the script is primarily consonant‑based; short vowels are usually omitted in everyday writing and added mentally by the reader.  

| Letter | Isolated Form | Name (English Approx.) | Approx. Sound |
|--------|---------------|------------------------|--------------|
| ا      | ا             | Alif                   | /aː/ (long “a”) |
| ب      | ب             | Bāʼ                    | /b/ |
| ت      | ت             | Tāʼ                    | /t/ |
| ث      | ث             | Thāʼ (soft)            | /θ/ as in “think” |
| ج      | ج             | Jīm                    | /dʒ/ as in “jam” |
| ح      | ح             | Ḥāʼ (deep)             | /ħ/ a voiceless pharyngeal fricative |
| خ      | خ             | Khāʼ                   | /x/ as in German “Bach” |
| د      | د             | Dāl                    | /d/ |
| ذ      | ذ             | Dhāl                   | /ð/ as in “this” |
| ر      | ر             | Rāʼ                    | /r/ (rolled) |
| ز      | ز             | Zayn                   | /z/ |
| س      | س             | Sīn                    | /s/ |
| ش      | ش             | Shīn                   | /ʃ/ as in “shoe” |
| ص      | ص             | Ṣād (emphatic)         | /sˤ/ |
| ض      | ض             | Ḍād (emphatic)         | /dˤ/ |
| ط      | ط             | Ṭāʼ (emphatic)         | /tˤ/ |
| ظ      | ظ             | Ẓāʼ (emphatic)         | /ðˤ/ |
| ع      | ع             | ‘Ayn (guttural)        | /ʕ/ a voiced pharyngeal fricative |
| غ      | غ             | Ghayn                  | /ɣ/ |
| ف      | ف             | Fāʼ                    | /f/ |
| ق      | ق             | Qāf                    | /q/ (uvular stop) |
| ك      | ك             | Kāf                    | /k/ |
| ل      | ل             | Lām                    | /l/ |
| م      | م             | Mīm                    | /m/ |
| ن      | ن             | Nūn                    | /n/ |
| ه      | ه             | Hāʼ                    | /h/ |
| و      | و             | Wāw                    | /w/ or long /uː/ |
| ي      | ي             | Yāʼ                    | /j/ or long /iː/ |
| ء      | ء             | Hamza (glottal stop)   | /ʔ/ |
| ﻻ      | لا            | Lām‑Alif (ligature)    | /laː/ |

> **Tip:** When you first meet a new letter, trace its isolated shape with your finger while saying its sound aloud. The physical motion supports memory.

---

## 2. Pronouncing the 28 Letters  

### 2.1 Vowel‑Free Consonants  

Most Arabic letters represent consonants that are either **voiced** (vocal cords vibrate) or **voiceless** (no vibration). Some have a “deep” or “emphatic” quality, produced by retracting the tongue toward the throat.  

- **Emphatic consonants** (ص, ض, ط, ظ) are pronounced like their non‑emphatic counterparts but with the tongue slightly retracted, giving a heavier sound.
- **Guttural letters** (ح, خ, ع, غ, ء) are articulated in the throat. Practice them in front of a mirror; you’ll notice the throat’s movement.

### 2.2 The Three “Th” Sounds  

English speakers often confuse the three Arabic “th” letters:

| Letter | Sound | English Approximation |
|--------|-------|-----------------------|
| ث | /θ/ | “think” |
| ذ | /ð/ | “this” |
| ظ | /ðˤ/ | emphatic version of “this” (rare in English) |

### 2.3 The Long Vowels (Alif, Waw, Ya)  

Although the alphabet consists of consonants, **Alif (ا)**, **Waw (و)**, and **Ya (ي)** also serve as **long vowels** when they appear without a diacritic (short‑vowel mark).  

- **Alif** → /aː/ as in “father”.  
- **Waw** → /uː/ as in “food”.  
- **Ya** → /iː/ as in “see”.  

These long vowels are pronounced **once** and held slightly longer than short vowels (see the next section).

---

## 3. Short Vowels: The Hidden Backbone  

Arabic scripts for beginners usually omit short vowels, but they are vital for correct pronunciation. Short vowels are represented by **diacritics** placed **above or below** the consonant. They are not separate letters; they merely modify the sound of the preceding consonant.

| Diacritic | Symbol | Name (English) | Sound | Example (Transliteration) |
|-----------|--------|----------------|-------|---------------------------|
|  ــَـ  | َ | **Fatha** | /a/ (as in “cat”) | **بَ** → *ba* |
|  ــِـ  | ِ | **Kasra** | /i/ (as in “see”) | **بِ** → *bi* |
|  ــُـ  | ُ | **Damma** | /u/ (as in “food”) | **بُ** → *bu* |
|  ــْـ  | ْ | **Sukun** (no vowel) | – | **بْ** → *b* (consonant alone) |
|  ــًـ  | ً | **Fathatan** (nunation) – used in formal writing, not needed for travel | – | — |
|  ــٍـ  | ٍ | **Kasratan** – same note as above | – | — |
|  ــٌـ  | ٌ | **Dammatan** – same note as above | – | — |

### 3.1 How Short Vowels Affect Meaning  

A single consonant skeleton can host multiple meanings depending on the short vowels inserted. For travelers, the most common words are short and heavily reliant on vowel patterns, so mastering the three diacritics is essential.

**Example:**  
- **كـتـب** (ktb) can become:  

  - **كَتَبَ** (*kataba*) – “he wrote”  
  - **كُتِبَ** (*kutiba*) – “it was written”  
  - **كِتَاب** (*kitāb*) – “book”  

The consonant framework stays the same; the vowel marks change the word entirely.

### 3.2 Quick Practice Exercise  

Write the isolated letter **م** (Mīm). Add each short‑vowel diacritic and say the resulting syllable aloud:

1. **مَ** → *ma* (as in “ma‑ma”)  
2. **مِ** → *mi* (as in “me”)  
3. **مُ** → *mu* (as in “moo”)  

Repeat until the sounds feel natural. This three‑step drill will be your “vowel warm‑up” before reading any new word.

---

## 4. Reading and Writing in Isolated Form  

When you first learn Arabic, you encounter each letter in its **isolated** shape—the form shown in the alphabet table above. Later, letters join to create cursive words; but mastering the isolated forms gives you a solid foundation and lets you read **signs, menus, and name tags** that often isolate letters for clarity (especially in tourist areas).

### 4.1 Writing the Alphabet  

1. **Start at the top right** of the page (remember the right‑to‑left direction).  
2. **Write each letter** in its isolated form, placing the short‑vowel diacritic **above** (fatha, damma) or **below** (kasra) the letter.  
3. **Practice the sequence**:  
   - Write **ا** (Alif) → **ب** (Bā) → **ت** (Tā) → **ث** (Thā) → … → **ي** (Yā).  

   This linear exercise reinforces the order and the direction of writing.

### 4.2 Simple Words for Travelers  

Below are ten everyday words you’ll meet on a trip, each presented in isolated letters with short‑vowel marks. Pronounce each syllable slowly, then blend them together.

| Arabic (isolated) | Transliteration | Meaning |
|-------------------|-----------------|----------|
| **ق ه و ة** | qahwa | coffee |
| **م س ر** | masr | Egypt (country name) |
| **س ب ح** | sabḥ | morning |
| **م ط ر** | maṭar | airport |
| **ب ر د** | bard | cold (weather) |
| **م ي س** | mis | (as in “Mıs” – not a common word, just for practice) |
| **ف ي ر** | fīr | (fictional placeholder) |
| **ط ل ع** | ṭalaʿ | to rise (e.g., sunrise) |
| **د ر ك** | darak | (fictional) |
| **ن ه ر** | nahr | river |

*Note:* The above “fictional” entries illustrate how any consonant cluster can be vocalized with short vowels. In real travel situations, you’ll encounter words like **مطار** (*maṭār* – “airport”) or **قهوة** (*qahwa* – “coffee”). The key is to spot the consonant skeleton and then supply the appropriate vowels.

### 4.3 Reading a Real‑World Sign  

Imagine a street sign that reads **م ط ر** with a small **fatha** under the **م** and a **damma** over the **ط**.  

- **مَ** → *ma*  
- **طُ** → *ṭu*  
- **ر** → *r* (no vowel, so the preceding vowel carries over)  

Combine: **maṭur** → actually pronounced **maṭār** (the long *ā* is implied). This is the word for “airport.” Knowing that **ا** (Alif) can be omitted in short‑vowel writing helps you infer the long vowel.

---

## 5. Transliteration: Bridging Arabic Script and Latin Letters  

Transliteration is a system that maps Arabic sounds to the Latin alphabet, making it easier for beginners to read and pronounce words without mastering the script first. Several schemes exist; the one used here follows **ISO 233‑2** with a few learner‑friendly adjustments.

| Arabic Letter | Common Transliteration | Example Word |
|---------------|-----------------------|--------------|
| ا | a (long) | **قهوة** → *qahwa* |
| ب | b | **بيت** → *bayt* |
| ت | t | **تَ** → *ta* |
| ث | th | **ثَ** → *tha* |
| ج | j | **جَ** → *ja* |
| ح | ḥ | **حَ** → *ḥa* |
| خ | kh | **خَ** → *kha* |
| د | d | **دَ** → *da* |
| ذ | dh | **ذَ** → *dha* |
| ر | r | **رَ** → *ra* |
| ز | z | **زَ** → *za* |
| س | s | **سَ** → *sa* |
| ش | sh | **شَ** → *sha* |
| ص | ṣ | **صَ** → *ṣa* |
| ض | ḍ | **ضَ** → *ḍa* |
| ط | ṭ | **طَ** → *ṭa* |
| ظ | ẓ | **ظَ** → *ẓa* |
| ع | ‘ | **عَ** → *‘a* |
| غ | gh | **غَ** → *gha* |
| ف | f | **فَ** → *fa* |
| ق | q | **قَ** → *qa* |
| ك | k | **كَ** → *ka* |
| ل | l | **لَ** → *la* |
| م | m | **مَ** → *ma* |
| ن | n | **نَ** → *na* |
| ه | h | **هَ** → *ha* |
| و | w / ū | **و** → *w* (consonant) or *ū* (long vowel) |
| ي | y / ī | **ي** → *y* (consonant) or *ī* (long vowel) |
| ء | ’ | **ء** → *’* (glottal stop) |

**Why Transliteration Matters for Travelers**  

- **Quick lookup**: When you see a word on a menu or a bus schedule, you can instantly map it to a pronunciation you already know.  
- **Pronunciation guide**: The symbols (ʿ, ḥ, ṣ, etc.) highlight sounds that have no exact English equivalent, prompting you to practice them.  
- **Confidence booster**: Being able to read the Latin version first reduces anxiety before confronting the Arabic script.

### 5.1 Transliteration Cheat Sheet  

- **ʾ** – Hamza (glottal stop) – think of the break in “uh‑oh”.  
- **ʿ** – ‘Ayn – a deep throat sound; practice by whispering “uh” while constricting the throat.  
- **ḥ** – Hard “h” – exhale strongly, as in “aha!” without vocal cords vibrating.  
- **kh** – Like the “ch” in German “Bach” or Scottish “loch”.  
- **sh** – Same as English “sh”.  
- **dh** – Like “th” in “this”.  
- **th** – Like “th” in “think”.  
- **s, ṣ** – *ṣ* is heavier; try saying *s* while pulling the tongue slightly back.  

---

## 6. Putting the Pieces Together: A Mini‑Practice Session  

### 6.1 Step‑by‑Step Reading Exercise  

You have the following three‑letter sign on a taxi stand:

```
ق   ر   ي
   َ   ِ
```

1. Identify each isolated letter: **ق** (qāf), **ر** (rā), **ي** (yā).  
2. Apply the diacritics: **قَ** (*qa*), **رِ** (*ri*), **ي** (no diacritic → acts as a consonant *y*).  
3. Blend the sounds: *qa + ri + y* → **qariy** → actually pronounced **qary** meaning “village” (قري).  

In a travel context, you might see **قري** on a map indicating a small settlement. Recognizing the letters and diacritics lets you understand the location instantly.

### 6.2 Writing Your Own Word  

Pick a simple travel word you already know in English, such as **“taxi.”** Its Arabic counterpart is **تاكسي** (*tāksī*). Write it in isolated form with short vowels:

- **ت** + **َ** → *ta* (fatha)  
- **ا** (long *ā*) → *ā* (no diacritic needed)  
- **ك** + **ِ** → *ki* (kasra)  
- **س** + **ِ** → *si* (kasra)  
- **ي** (long *ī*) → *ī*  

Resulting isolated sequence: **تَ ا كِ سِ ي**. Practicing this reinforces the connection between the transliteration *tāksī* and the script.

### 6.3 Listening Check  

Ask a native speaker (or a language app) to say **قهوة** (*qahwa*). Record the audio, then try to write the word using isolated letters and short vowels. Compare your transcription to the recorded pronunciation. This loop of **listen → write → compare** solidifies both auditory and visual recognition.

---

## 7. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Quick Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----------|
| **Confusing fatha and damma** (mixing *a* and *u* sounds) | The diacritics look similar; both are small marks placed above the letter. | Associate **‑َ** (fatha) with the word “**cat**” (a) and **‑ُ** (damma) with “**food**” (u). Say the English word while visualizing the diacritic. |
| **Skipping the sukun** (thinking a consonant always has a vowel) | Beginners often add an implied vowel automatically. | Remember that **‑ْ** means “no vowel.” Practice by saying the consonant alone, like **بْ** → *b* (as in “b‑” sound before a pause). |
| **Pronouncing emphatic letters like their non‑emphatic counterparts** | The subtle tongue retraction is hard to feel at first. | Place the tip of your tongue on the roof of your mouth, then pull it slightly back while saying **ص** (*ṣ*). Feel the difference in resonance. |
| **Relying solely on transliteration** | Transliteration hides the visual shape of letters, making script recognition slower. | Pair each transliterated word with its isolated‑letter representation during practice. |
| **Writing letters left‑to‑right** | Habit from Latin scripts overrides Arabic direction. | Use a **right‑to‑left writing ruler** (a simple piece of paper with a vertical line) to keep your hand on the correct side of the page. |

---

## 8. Practical Tips for the Traveling Learner  

1. **Carry a pocket cheat sheet** with the isolated alphabet and diacritics. A single A5 page (front and back) fits easily in a passport holder.  
2. **Label everyday objects** in your hotel room with the Arabic word (e.g., **سرير** *sarīr* for “bed”). Seeing the script repeatedly reinforces memory.  
3. **Use smartphone camera OCR** (optical character recognition) apps that can read Arabic signs and display transliteration. This is a safety net, but try to guess the word first!  
4. **Practice “vowel filling”**: When you see a word without diacritics, pause and mentally insert short vowels before checking a dictionary. This habit improves fluency.  
5. **Listen to local radio** for short phrases. Even if you don’t understand the content, hearing the rhythm of Arabic vowels helps internalize pronunciation patterns.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- Arabic has **28 consonantal letters**; each appears in an **isolated form** that you must learn before connecting them in cursive.  
- **Short vowels** (fatha, kasra, damma) are diacritics that give life to the consonant skeleton; mastering them enables accurate pronunciation of everyday words.  
- **Long vowels** are represented by the letters **Alif, Waw, Ya** when they appear without diacritics.  
- Transliteration provides a bridge for beginners, but pairing it with the actual script accelerates reading ability.  
- Regular, focused practice—writing isolated letters, adding diacritics, and reading simple travel‑related words—builds the confidence needed to order coffee, ask for directions, and navigate Arabic‑speaking environments.

modules.title: Greetings, Politeness, and Small Talk
modules.content:
## Warm‑up: The First Encounter  

Imagine you step off the bus in Marrakech, the sun is high, and a shopkeeper greets you with a friendly smile. Your first words can set the tone for the whole visit. Knowing **how to say “hello,” “please,” and “thank you”** in Arabic will instantly make you appear courteous and approachable.

---

## Common Greetings  

### Formal vs. informal  

Arabic distinguishes between formal and informal greetings, much like English “Good morning” vs. “Hey.” In most tourist settings, a **neutral greeting** works everywhere.

| Arabic (script) | Transliteration | When to use |
|-----------------|----------------|-------------|
| **Marhaban** | *marḥabān* | General “hello,” safe for strangers. |
| **Ahlan** | *ahlān* | Slightly more informal, like “hi.” |
| **As-salām ‘alaykum** | *as‑salaam ‘alaykum* | Very respectful, literally “peace be upon you.” Often answered with **Wa‑‘alaykum as‑salaam**. |
| **Sabāḥ al‑khayr** | *sabāḥ al‑khair* | “Good morning.” |
| **Masā’ al‑khayr** | *masā’ al‑khair* | “Good evening.” |

> **Tip:** The diacritics you learned in *Arabic Sounds and Script Foundations* (fatha, damma, kasra) tell you the short vowel sounds. For *marḥabān* the fatha on **م** gives “ma‑,” the sukun on **ر** stops the sound, and the fatha on **ح** yields “‑ḥa‑.”  

### Pronunciation pointers  

- **ح** (ḥ) is a **guttural** consonant; it is pronounced deeper in the throat than the English “h.”  
- **ص** (ṣ) in **as‑salaam** is an **emphatic** consonant; give it a slightly heavier, more rounded quality.  
- **ʿ** (ʿayn) in **‘alaykum** is another guttural sound—think of a brief catch in the throat.  

Practicing these sounds will make your greetings sound natural and respectful.

---

## Asking “How are you?” and Responding  

### The question  

| Arabic (script) | Transliteration | Gender |
|-----------------|----------------|--------|
| **Kayfa ḥāluk?** | *kayfa ḥāluk?* | Male |
| **Kayfa ḥālik?** | *kayfa ḥālik?* | Female |
| **Kayfa ḥālukum?** | *kayfa ḥālukum?* | Plural (group) |

**Kayfa** means “how,” and **ḥāl** means “condition” or “state.” The ending **‑k** (male) or **‑ki** (female) agrees with the listener’s gender, a pattern you’ll encounter often in Arabic.

### Short answers  

- **Al‑ḥamdu lillāh, ana bikhayr.**  
  *Al‑ḥamdu lillāh, ana bikhayr.* – “Thanks to God, I am fine.”  
- **Lā ba‘d.** – “Not bad.”  
- **Ta‘bān/ta‘bāna** – “Tired” (male/female).  

You can add **wa‑anta?** (“and you?”) after your answer to keep the conversation flowing.

### Mini dialogue  

```
You:   Marhaban!
Shopkeeper: As‑salaam ‘alaykum.
You:   Wa‑‘alaykum as‑salaam. Kayfa ḥāluk?
Shopkeeper: Al‑ḥamdu lillāh, ana bikhayr. Wa‑anta?
You:   Ana bikhayr, shukran.
```

Notice the **exchange of greetings** before the “how are you?” question—this mirrors everyday Arabic politeness.

---

## Polite Expressions  

### Please  

| Arabic (script) | Transliteration | Note |
|-----------------|----------------|------|
| **Min faḍlik** | *min faḍlik* | To a male. |
| **Min faḍliki** | *min faḍliki* | To a female. |
| **Law samaḥt** | *law samaḥt* | “If you please,” a softer, more indirect way. |

**Min** means “from,” and **faḍl** means “favor.” The phrase literally asks for a favor, which is why it works as “please.”

### Thank you  

- **Shukran** – “Thank you.”  
- **Shukran jiddan** – “Thank you very much.”  

### Excuse me / Sorry  

| Arabic (script) | Transliteration | Usage |
|-----------------|----------------|-------|
| **‘Afwan** | *‘afwan* | “Excuse me” (to get attention) or “You’re welcome.” |
| **‘Āsif** | *‘āsif* | “I’m sorry” (more sincere apology). |
| **‘Āsifa** | *‘āsifa* | Female form of “I’m sorry.” |

### Putting them together  

When you need a drink at a café:

1. **‘Afwan**, could I have **min faḍlik** a glass of water?  
2. Waiter brings it → **Shukran!**  
3. If you accidentally bump into someone → **‘Āsif**.  

These short formulas keep interactions smooth and show respect for the local culture.

---

## Introducing Yourself  

### Sentence pattern  

**Ana + [name] + min + [country].**  

- **Ana** – “I am.” (the pronoun you already know from earlier chapters)  
- **min** – “from.”  

**Example with gender agreement:**  

- **Ana Ismī Ahmed, min Miṣr.** – “My name is Ahmed, I am from Egypt.”  
- **Ana Ismī Laila, min Al‑ʿArabiyyah.** – “My name is Laila, I am from the Arab world.”  

For a more casual introduction, you can say **Ismi …** (“My name is …”) before adding the nationality.

### Practice set  

| English | Arabic (script) | Transliteration |
|---------|----------------|-----------------|
| My name is Sam, I am from the United Kingdom. | اسمي سام، من المملكة المتحدة. | *Ismī Sām, min al‑Mamlakah al‑Muttaḥidah.* |
| My name is Fatima, I am from Saudi Arabia. | اسمي فاطمة، من السعودية. | *Ismī Fāṭimah, min as‑Sa‘ūdiyyah.* |
| I am John, from Canada. | أنا جون، من كندا. | *Ana Jūn, min Kanadā.* |

Remember the **right‑to‑left** direction of Arabic script when writing these sentences, and place the diacritics (if you use them) above or below the letters as you learned.

---

## Mini Dialogue: At a Café  

Below is a realistic conversation that strings together everything covered so far. Read it aloud, paying attention to the pronunciation cues.

```
You (entering): Marhaban!
Barista: As‑salaam ‘alaykum.
You: Wa‑‘alaykum as‑salaam. Kayfa ḥāluk?
Barista: Al‑ḥamdu lillāh, ana bikhayr. Wa‑anta?
You: Ana bikhayr, shukran. Ismi Sara, min Al‑Jazā’ir.
Barista: Marḥaban Sara! Min faḍlik, shāy bi‑sukkar?
You: ‘Afwan, law samaḥt, shāy bidoon sukkar.
Barista: Hādhā al‑shāy. Shukran jiddan.
You: Shukran. ‘Āsif, al‑ma‘a qaleel?
Barista: La, al‑ma‘a kīfiyyah. Taqaddam?
You: Na‘am, shukran.
```

Key points highlighted:

- **Greeting exchange** → **Marhaban**, **As‑salaam ‘alaykum**.  
- **“How are you?”** with gender‑appropriate form (**ḥāluk**).  
- **Self‑introduction** using **Ismi** and **min**.  
- **Polite request** with **min faḍlik** and **law samaḥt**.  
- **Thank you** and **excuse me** placed naturally.  

Practicing this dialogue will give you a ready‑made script for many travel situations.

---

## Cultural Note: Greeting Etiquette  

- **Handshakes** are common among men, but some women may prefer a slight nod.  
- In more traditional settings, a **light cheek kiss** (usually on the right cheek) is customary among close acquaintances.  
- Always use the **male form** (**‑k**) when speaking to a mixed‑gender group unless you know the gender of each individual.  
- When addressing someone older or of higher status, adding **“please” (min faḍlik)** and **“thank you” (shukran)** enhances respect.

---

## Practice Exercises  

1. **Fill in the blanks** with the appropriate greeting or polite phrase.  

   a. ___ (Good evening), ___ (please) give me a map.  
   b. ___ (Excuse me), ___ (thank you very much) for the help.  

2. **Match the Arabic sentence to its English meaning.**  

   - أَسْلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ                 a. “My name is Tom, I am from Australia.”  
   - مَرْحَبًا، كَيْفَ حَالُكِ؟          b. “Good morning.”  
   - اسمي مريم، من لبنان.                c. “Peace be upon you.”  
   - صَبَاحُ الخَيْر                     d. “How are you?”  

3. **Create a short self‑introduction** in Arabic, including name, nationality, and a polite “thank you” for listening.  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Marhaban**, **Ahlan**, and **As‑salaam ‘alaykum** are the core greetings; choose based on formality.  
- Use **kayfa ḥāluk/ḥālik** to ask “how are you?” and respond with **al‑ḥamdu lillāh, ana bikhayr** or similar short answers.  
- Politeness words: **min faḍlik** (please), **shukran** (thank you), **‘afwan** and **‘āsif** (excuse me / sorry).  
- Introduce yourself with **Ana [Name] min [Country]** or **Ismi [Name]**, keeping gender agreement in mind.  
- Practice the integrated dialogue to build confidence for real‑world encounters.

modules.title: Numbers, Dates, and Time
modules.content:
## Counting from Zero to One Hundred  

Imagine you’ve just arrived at a bustling souk. The vendor greets you with a smile and asks, “كم عدد التفاح؟” *Kam ‘adad al‑tuffāḥ?* “How many apples?”  
To answer confidently you need the numbers from **0 – 100**.  

### Arabic Numerals vs. Words  
Arabic uses two parallel systems:  

* **Arabic‑Indic digits** (٠ ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥ ٦ ٧ ٨ ٩) – the symbols you’ll see on price tags, clocks, and receipts.  
* **Spoken words** – the forms you’ll pronounce in conversation.  

Both are read **right‑to‑left**, just like the script you learned in *Arabic Sounds and Script Foundations*.  

### The Base Numbers (0‑10)  

| Digit | Word (transliteration) | Note |
|-------|------------------------|------|
| ٠ | **ṣifr** (صفر) | “zero” – used in phone numbers, prices, etc. |
| ١ | ** wāḥid** (واحد) | masculine “one”; ** wāḥida** (واحدة) for feminine nouns |
| ₂ | ** ithnān** (اثنان) | “two” – note the short vowel *i* (kasra) |
| ٣ | ** thalātha** (ثلاثة) | “three” |
| ٤ | ** arba‘a** (أربعة) | “four” |
| ٥ | ** khamsa** (خمسة) | “five” |
| ٦ | ** sitta** (ستة) | “six” |
| ٧ | ** sab‘a** (سبعة) | “seven” |
| ٨ | ** thamāniya** (ثمانية) | “eight” |
| ٩ | ** tis‘a** (تسعة) | “nine” |
| ١٠ | ** ‘ashara** (عشرة) | “ten” |

> **Tip:** The vowel markings you saw earlier (fatha, kasra, damma) guide pronunciation. For example, **ثلاثة** carries a *fatha* on the *ث* (thā) and a *kasra* on the *ا* (ā).

### Forming the Teens (11‑19)  

Arabic builds 11‑19 by placing **‘ashar** after the unit, but the order is **unit + ‘ashar**.  

| Number | Word | Literal pattern |
|--------|------|-----------------|
| 11 | **ahad ‘ashar** (أحد عشر) | “one‑ten” |
| 12 | **ithnā ‘ashar** (اثنا عشر) | “two‑ten” |
| 13 | **thalātha ‘ashar** (ثلاثة عشر) | “three‑ten” |
| … | … | … |
| 19 | **tis‘a ‘ashar** (تسعة عشر) | “nine‑ten” |

### Tens (20, 30 … 90)  

| Digit | Word | Approx. English |
|-------|------|-----------------|
| ٢٠ | **‘ishrūn** (عشرون) | twenty |
| ٣٠ | **thalāthūn** (ثلاثون) | thirty |
| ٤٠ | **arba‘ūn** (أربعون) | forty |
| ٥٠ | **khamsūn** (خمسون) | fifty |
| ٦٠ | **sittūn** (ستون) | sixty |
| ٧٠ | **sab‘ūn** (سبعون) | seventy |
| ٨٠ | **thamānūn** (ثمانون) | eighty |
| ٩٠ | **tis‘ūn** (تسعون) | ninety |

### Combining Tens and Units (21‑99)  

The pattern is **unit + wa + ten** (the conjunction *wa* = “and”).  

Example:  

* ٢١ → ** wāḥid wa ‘ishrūn** (واحد وعشرون) “one and twenty” → 21  
* ٤٥ → **khamsa wa arba‘ūn** (خمسة وأربعون) “five and forty” → 45  

> **Note:** When the unit is a **feminine noun** (e.g., *سُكّر* “sugar”), the number itself takes the feminine form (e.g., **خمسة** stays the same, but *one* becomes **واحدة**).  

### The Hundred  

| Digit | Word | Usage |
|-------|------|-------|
| ١٠٠ | **mi’a** (مئة) | “one hundred” |
| ٢٠٠ | **mi’atān** (مئتان) | “two hundred” |
| ٣٠٠‑٩٠٠ | **mi’a + unit** (e.g., **ثلاثمئة** *thalāthumi’a* “three hundred”) |

Now you can count any price on a market stall, read a bus schedule, or negotiate a hotel rate.

---

## Naming Days, Months, and Years  

### The Calendar in Arabic  

Arabic‑speaking countries use the **Gregorian calendar** for civil life, and many also reference the **Hijri (Islamic) calendar** for religious dates. For travel purposes, the Gregorian names will be sufficient.  

### Days of the Week  

| Arabic | Transliteration | Literal meaning |
|--------|----------------|-----------------|
| الأحد | **al‑aḥad** | “the first” |
| الإثنين | **al‑ithnayn** | “the second” |
| الثلاثاء | **ath‑thulāthā’** | “the third” |
| الأربعاء | **al‑arba‘ā’** | “the fourth” |
| الخميس | **al‑khamīs** | “the fifth” |
| الجمعة | **al‑jum‘a** | “the gathering” |
| السبت | **as‑sab‘a** | “the seventh” |

> **Tip:** The definite article **al-** (ال) is attached to each day; you will hear the article in everyday speech.

### Months of the Year  

| Arabic | Transliteration |
|--------|----------------|
| يناير | **Yanāyir** |
| فبراير | **Fibrāyir** |
| مارس | **Māris** |
| أبريل | **Abrīl** |
| مايو | **Māyū** |
| يونيو | **Yūniyū** |
| يوليو | **Yūliyū** |
| أغسطس | **Aghustus** |
| سبتمبر | **Sibtambar** |
| أكتوبر | **Uktūbar** |
| نوفمبر | **Nūfimbir** |
| ديسمبر | **Dīsambar** |

These are pronounced close to their English counterparts, with Arabic vowel quality (e.g., *ū* as in “food”).

### Stating a Full Date  

The typical order is **day – month – year** (same as English).  

**Example:** 15 April 2024  

*Arabic:* **١٥ أبريل ٢٠٢٤** (digit form)  
*Spoken:* **al‑khamsata ‘ashar min April sana 2024**  
Literally: “the fifteen of April year two‑zero‑two‑four.”

When using words for the year, you can say:  

* **سنة ألفين وأربعة وعشرون** (*sanat al‑alfayn wa‑arba‘a wa‑‘asharūn*) – “the year two thousand twenty‑four.”  

> **Tip:** For quick conversation, using the Arabic‑Indic digits for the year is perfectly acceptable.

---

## Asking and Understanding the Current Time  

### Telling Time in Arabic  

Arabic uses a 12‑hour clock, usually accompanied by **صباحًا** (*ṣabāḥan* “in the morning”) or **مساءً** (*masā’an* “in the evening”).  

| English | Arabic | Literal |
|---------|--------|---------|
| 1:00 am | **الساعة الواحدة صباحًا** (*as‑sā‘a al‑wāḥida ṣabāḥan*) |
| 3:30 pm | **الساعة الثالثة والنصف مساءً** (*as‑sā‘a ath‑thalātha wa‑an‑niṣf masā’an*) |
| 12:00 noon | **الساعة الثانية عشرة ظهرًا** (*as‑sā‘a ath‑thānīya ‘ashara ẓuhran*) |

**Structure:** **الساعة** (*as‑sā‘a* “the hour”) + **number** + optional **و + fraction** + **time‑of‑day marker**.  

#### Common Fractions  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| نصف | **an‑niṣf** | half |
| ربع | **rub‘** | quarter |
| ثلاثة أرباع | **thalātha ar‑rub‘** | three‑quarters |

### Practical Dialogue: Checking Opening Hours  

> **You:** *ما هو وقت فتح المتجر اليوم؟*  
> *Ma huwa waqt fataḥ al‑mutajar al‑yawm?* – “What time does the shop open today?”  

> **Shopkeeper:** *المتجر يفتح الساعة الثامنة صباحًا.*  
> *Al‑mutajar yaftaḥ as‑sā‘a ath‑thāmina ṣabāḥan.* – “The shop opens at 8 am.”  

> **You:** *وكم يغلق؟*  
> *Wa kam yughliq?* – “And when does it close?”  

> **Shopkeeper:** *يغلق الساعة الخامسة مساءً.*  
> *Yughliq as‑sā‘a al‑khāmisa masā’an.* – “It closes at 5 pm.”  

### Listening for Numbers in Time  

When you hear a time expressed with **Arabic‑Indic digits**, remember they read right‑to‑left.  

* Example on a digital clock: **٠٨:٤٥** = 08:45.  
* The spoken form would be **الساعة الثامنة وخمس وأربعون دقيقة مساءً** (*as‑sā‘a ath‑thāmina wa‑khamsa wa‑arba‘ūn daqīqa masā’an*).  

---

## Simple Price Negotiations & Currency  

### The Arabic Word for Money  

* **مال** (*māl*) – “money” (general)  
* **سعر** (*si‘r*) – “price”  
* **دولار** (*dūlār*) – “dollar” (used in many Arab countries)  
* **ريال** (*riyāl*) – “riyal” (Saudi, Qatari, etc.)  
* **جنيه** (*junayh*) – “pound” (Egyptian, Sudanese)  

### Expressing Prices  

The pattern is **number + currency**.  

* **٥٠٠ ريال** – *khams mi’a riyāl* – “five hundred riyals”  
* **٢٠ دولارًا** – *‘ishrūn dūlārān* – “twenty dollars”  

**Note:** The noun *dollar* is masculine, so the number takes the masculine form (e.g., *‘ishrūn*).  

### Common Negotiation Phrases  

| English | Arabic | Transliteration |
|---------|--------|-----------------|
| How much is this? | بكم هذا؟ | *bikam hādhā?* |
| Is the price fixed? | السعر ثابت؟ | *as‑si‘r thābit?* |
| Can you lower the price? | هل يمكنك أن تخفض السعر؟ | *hal yumkinuka an tukhaffid as‑si‘r?* |
| I’ll give you… | أعطيك… | *a‘ṭīk…* |
| That’s too expensive. | هذا غالي جداً. | *hādhā ghālī jiddan.* |

### Sample Bargaining Scenario  

> **You:** *بكم هذا السجادة؟*  
> *Bikam hādhā as‑sajjāda?* – “How much is this rug?”  

> **Vendor:** *السجادة مئتان وخمسون ريال.*  
> *As‑sajjāda mi’atān wa‑khamsūn riyāl.* – “The rug is 250 riyals.”  

> **You:** *هل يمكنك أن تخفض السعر إلى مئتين؟*  
> *Hal yumkinuka an tukhaffid as‑si‘r ilā mi’atayn?* – “Can you lower the price to 200?”  

> **Vendor:** *حسنًا، مئتين وخمسون.*  
> *Ḥasanān, mi’atayn wa‑khamsūn.* – “Alright, 250.”  

> **You:** *إلى مئتين وخمسين، أوافق.*  
> *Ilā mi’atayn wa‑khamsīn, awāfiq.* – “To 250, I agree.”  

> **Vendor:** *تم. شكراً!*  
> *Tam. Shukran!* – “Done. Thank you!”  

By mastering the numbers and the short phrases above, you’ll feel comfortable handling most price talks.

---

## Practice Exercises  

### 1. Fill‑in the Blanks  

Translate the following into Arabic (use digits where appropriate).  

1. “I need **seven** tickets.” → _______________________  
2. “The train leaves at **9 : 15 am**.” → _______________________  
3. “Today's date is **23 September 2023**.” → _______________________  
4. “How much is **three hundred** dollars?” → _______________________  

### 2. Listening Drill  

Listen to a native speaker (audio file provided in the companion app) saying three different times. Write the digital representation you hear.  

1. **الساعة الثانية عشرة والنصف مساءً** → ________  
2. **الساعة السابعة وخمس دقائق صباحًا** → ________  
3. **الساعة العاشرة ربع مساءً** → ________  

### 3. Role‑Play  

Partner A: Tourist asking for opening hours of a museum.  
Partner B: Museum attendant.  

Use at least three of the time‑related phrases from the “Checking Opening Hours” dialogue. Switch roles after one round.

---

## Cultural Note: Numbers in Public Signage  

In many Arab countries, public signs (bus timetables, price boards, hotel check‑in counters) display both **Arabic‑Indic digits** and **Western Arabic numerals** (0‑9). This dual display helps visitors who may not be familiar with the Arabic script. When you see a sign like **٠٨:٠٠**, you can safely read it as “08:00.”  

---

## Frequently Asked Questions  

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| **Do I need to memorize the Arabic words for every number up to 100?** | No. Learn the base numbers (0‑10), the tens (20‑90), and the pattern for combining them. This covers all numbers up to 100. |
| **Is it okay to use English numbers when speaking Arabic?** | In informal settings, many locals understand Western numerals, especially in tourist areas. However, using Arabic words shows respect and improves fluency. |
| **What if I forget the gender agreement for a number?** | When unsure, use the masculine form—it is accepted for mixed‑gender groups and most inanimate objects. |
| **How do I ask for the time politely?** | *ما هو الوقت الآن؟* (*ma huwa al‑waqt al‑ān?*) – “What time is it now?” Adding *من فضلك* (*min faḍlik*) makes it even more courteous. |

---

## Putting It All Together: Mini Dialogue  

> **You (tourist):** *مرحبًا، هل يمكنك أن تخبرني عن مواعيد القطار اليوم؟*  
> *Marḥaban, hal yumkinuka an tukbirnī ‘an mawā‘īd al‑qiṭār al‑yawm?* – “Hello, can you tell me the train schedule for today?”  

> **Station Clerk:** *القِطار يغادر الساعة السابعة والنصف صباحًا، ويصل إلى المدينة في الساعة العاشرة.*  
> *Al‑qiṭār yughaḍir as‑sā‘a as‑sābi‘a wa‑an‑niṣf ṣabāḥan, wa‑yasil ilā al‑madīna fī as‑sā‘a al‑‘āshira.* – “The train departs at 7 : 30 am and arrives in the city at 10 am.”  

> **You:** *شكراً. كم سعر التذكرة؟*  
> *Shukran. Kam si‘r at‑tadhkira?* – “Thank you. How much is the ticket?”  

> **Clerk:** *السعر مئتان وخمسون ريال.*  
> *As‑si‘r mi’atayn wa‑khamsūn riyāl.* – “The price is 250 riyals.”  

> **You:** *هل يمكن أن أخفضه إلى مئتين؟*  
> *Hal yumkin an ukhfidhu ilā mi’atayn?* – “Can you lower it to 200?”  

> **Clerk:** *حسنًا، مئتين وخمسون.*  
> *Ḥasanān, mi’atayn wa‑khamsūn.* – “Okay, 250.”  

> **You:** *إلى مئتين وخمسين. أوافق.*  
> *Ilā mi’atayn wa‑khamsīn. Awāfiq.* – “To 250, I agree.”  

> **Clerk:** *تم. رحلة سعيدة!*  
> *Tam. Riḥla sa‘īda!* – “Done. Have a good trip!”  

---

## ## Key Takeaways  

- **Numbers 0‑100** are built from a handful of base words; combine units with *wa* (“and”) for 21‑99.  
- **Arabic‑Indic digits** (٠‑٩) appear on signs and receipts; reading them right‑to‑left is essential.  
- **Days and months** follow a simple order; the definite article *al-* prefixes each day.  
- **Dates** are expressed as **day – month – year**, using either digits or words.  
- **Time** uses the phrase **الساعة** + number + optional fraction + *صباحًا* / *مساءً*.  
- **Price negotiations** rely on the same number patterns; remember gender agreement for nouns.  
- Practice with real‑world dialogues—asking for opening hours, checking schedules, and bargaining—will cement these structures.  

With these tools, you can confidently navigate schedules, read signs, and handle money while traveling in the Arab world. Happy exploring!

modules.title: Navigating Transportation
modules.content:
## Where Are You Going?  —  Asking for Directions  

Imagine you have just arrived at Cairo International Airport and need to find the **Egyptian Museum**. The first person you meet is a taxi driver who looks friendly but you’re not sure how to tell him exactly where you want to go.  

The ability to **ask for directions**, **understand simple signboards**, and **communicate with drivers** will turn a confusing moment into a smooth experience. Below are the essential words, structures, and practice dialogues you need.

### Core Vocabulary  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English | Note |
|--------|----------------|---------|------|
| أين | **ayna** | where? | Question word introduced in earlier chapters |
| إلى | **ilā** | to / toward | Preposition used with verbs of motion |
| شارع | **shāriʿ** | street | |
| تقاطع | **taqāṭʿ** | intersection | |
| يمين | **yamīn** | right | |
| يسار | **yasār** | left | |
| أمام | **amām** | in front of | |
| خلف | **khalf** | behind | |
| قريب | **qarīb** | near | |
| بعيد | **baʿīd** | far | |
| محطة | **maḥaṭṭa** | station (bus, metro) | |
| باص / حافلة | **bāṣ / ḥāfila** | bus | two common terms |
| قطار | **qaṭār** | train | |
| مترو | **metro** | metro (subway) | borrowed word |
| تاكسي | **tāksī** | taxi | |
| أريد | **urīdu** | I want | verb “to want” from earlier verb patterns |
| كم؟ | **kam?** | how much? | uses the interrogative “how many” from Numbers chapter |
| سعر | **siʿr** | price / fare | |

### Simple Question Patterns  

1. **“Where is …?”**  

   - **أين … ؟** – **ayna … ?**  
   - Example: **أين المتحف المصري ؟** – **Ayna al-matḥaf al-miṣrī?** – “Where is the Egyptian Museum?”  

2. **“How do I get to …?”**  

   - **كيف أذهب إلى … ؟** – **kayfa ’adhhab ilā … ?**  
   - Example: **كيف أذهب إلى محطة المترو ؟** – “How do I get to the metro station?”  

3. **“Is it far?”**  

   - **هل هو بعيد ؟** – **hal huwa baʿīd?**  

4. **“Turn right/left at …”**  

   - **إ turn right:** **إ turn left**  
   - **انعطف يميناً عند …** – **iʿnaṭif yamīnan ʿinda …** – “Turn right at …”  
   - **انعطف يساراً عند …** – **iʿnaṭif yasārān ʿinda …** – “Turn left at …”

### Using Verbs of Motion  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| يذهب | **yadhhab** | he/she/it goes |
| يركب | **yarkab** | he/she/it rides (a vehicle) |
| يمشي | **yamshī** | he/she/it walks |
| ينتظر | **yantazir** | he/she/it waits |
| يوقف | **yuqif** | he/she/it stops |

*Tip:* When you combine a verb with the preposition **إلى** (to), the destination follows directly: **أريد أن أذهب إلى السوق** – “I want to go to the market.” The verb **أريد** (I want) was introduced in the “Greetings” chapter; you can now pair it with any location noun.

### Practice Dialogue – Asking a Local for Directions  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **المسافر:** عفواً، أين المتحف المصري؟ | **Al-musāfir:** ʿAfwan, ayna al-matḥaf al-miṣrī? | Excuse me, where is the Egyptian Museum? |
| **المسافر:** هل هو بعيد؟ | **Al-musāfir:** Hal huwa baʿīd? | Is it far? |
| **المواطن:** لا، ليس بعيداً. إذهب إلى شارع التحرير، ثم انعطف يميناً عند التقاطع. | **Al-mawṭin:** Lā, laysa baʿīdan. Iḏhab ilā shāriʿ al-taḥrīr, thumma iʿnaṭif yamīnan ʿinda al-taqāṭʿ. | No, it’s not far. Go to Tahrir Street, then turn right at the intersection. |
| **المسافر:** شكراً جزيلاً! | **Al-musāfir:** Shukran jazīlan! | Thank you very much! |

Notice the use of **إذهب** (go) and the directional verbs **انعطف يميناً** (turn right). The response also includes **ليس بعيداً** (not far), a useful phrase when you want to reassure a traveler.

---

## Reading Signboards and Road Signs  

Arabic signboards are often concise, using icons and a few words. Recognizing the most common words will let you navigate streets even without a local guide.

### Typical Road Sign Vocabulary  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| اتجاه | **ittijāh** | direction |
| خروج | **khurūj** | exit |
| دخول | **dukhūl** | entrance |
| منع | **manʿ** | prohibited |
| ممنوع | **mamnūʿ** | forbidden |
| موقف | **mawqif** | parking |
| موقف سيارات | **mawqif sayārāt** | car park |
| حظر | **ḥazr** | ban |
| سرعة | **sarʿa** | speed |
| حدود السرعة | **ḥudūd al-sarʿa** | speed limit |
| مشاة | **mashā** | pedestrians |
| أوقف | **awqif** | stop (imperative) |
| انتبه | **intabih** | beware / pay attention |

### Reading a Sample Sign  

> **موقف سيارات**  
> **ممنوع الوقوف أمام الباب**  

- **موقف سيارات** – **mawqif sayārāt** – “Car park”  
- **ممنوع الوقوف أمام الباب** – **mamnūʿ al-wuqūf amām al-bāb** – “No stopping in front of the door”

You can practice by scanning street photos in a travel guide or on a language‑learning app, noting the diacritics only when you feel comfortable. Remember, many signs omit short vowels; the context and the shape of the letters usually make the meaning clear.

### Quick Recognition Exercise  

Identify the meaning of each sign (write the English meaning on a piece of paper).  

1. **سرعة 50 كلم/س**  
2. **ممنوع دخول السيارات**  
3. **اتجه إلى اليمين**  

*Answers:* 1) Speed limit 50 km/h, 2) No entry for cars, 3) Turn right.

---

## Public Transportation: Buses, Metro, and Trains  

Most Arab cities have a network of **buses (حافلة / باص)**, **metro (مترو)**, and **trains (قطار)**. Below are the key verbs, nouns, and phrases you’ll need to buy a ticket, ask about routes, and understand announcements.

### Vocabulary for Public Transport  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| تذكرة | **tadhīra** | ticket |
| بطاقة | **biṭāqa** | pass / card |
| محطة | **maḥaṭṭa** | station |
| خط | **khatt** | line (e.g., metro line) |
| جدول | **jadwal** | schedule |
| موعد | **mawʿid** | time (appointment) |
| ساعة | **sāʿa** | hour |
| دقيقة | **daqīqa** | minute |
| متى؟ | **matā?** | when? |
| أين؟ | **ayna?** | where? |
| إلى أين؟ | **ilā ayna?** | to where? |
| كلّ الـ… | **kull al‑…** | every … (e.g., كلّ الساعة) |
| خفيف | **khafīf** | cheap / light (as in fare) |
| غالي | **ghālī** | expensive |

### Buying a Ticket – Sample Dialogue  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **المسافر:** بكم تذكرة إلى محطة القطار؟ | **Al-musāfir:** Bikam tadhīra ilā maḥaṭṭ al-qiṭār? | How much is a ticket to the train station? |
| **البائع:** ثلاثة جنيهات. | **Al-bāʿiʿ:** Thalātha junāhāt. | Three pounds. |
| **المسافر:** أريد واحدة، من فضلك. | **Al-musāfir:** Urīdu wāḥida, min faḍlik. | One, please. |
| **البائع:** تفضل. | **Al-bāʿiʿ:** Tafaddal. | Here you go. |

*Note:* The numeral **ثلاثة** (three) uses the Arabic numeral system introduced in the “Numbers” chapter. When speaking, you can also say **ثلاث جنيهات** (three pounds) without the formal numeral symbols.

### Asking About the Metro  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| ما هو خط المترو رقم … ؟ | **mā huwa khatt al‑metro raqam … ?** | Which metro line is number … ? |
| أين أقرب محطة؟ | **ayna aqrab maḥaṭṭa?** | Where is the nearest station? |
| هل يوجد قطار إلى … ؟ | **hal yūjad qiṭār ilā … ?** | Is there a train to … ? |
| متى يغادر القطار؟ | **matā yughādir al‑qiṭār?** | When does the train leave? |

### Understanding Announcements (Typical Phrases)  

- **القطار القادم إلى …** – **al‑qiṭār al‑qādim ilā …** – “The arriving train to …”  
- **الرجاء الوقوف خلف الخط الأصفر** – **al‑rajāʾ al‑wuqūf khalf al‑khatt al‑aṣfar** – “Please stand behind the yellow line”  
- **سيتم إغلاق البوابة في … دقيقة** – **sayatimm ʾighlāq al‑bawwāba fī … daqīqa** – “The gate will close in … minutes”

Listening to a few minutes of a metro announcement (often available on YouTube) will help you become comfortable with the cadence and the use of the verb **سيتم** (will be) plus the infinitive.

---

## Talking to Drivers – Taxis, Ride‑Sharing, and Private Cars  

When you hop into a **taxi (تاكسي)** or arrange a ride‑sharing service, you’ll need to be clear about the destination, negotiate the fare, and possibly ask for a receipt.

### Essential Phrases  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| إلى … من فضلك | **ilā … min faḍlik** | To …, please |
| كم الأجرة؟ | **kam al‑ʾujra?** | How much is the fare? |
| أريد إيصالاً | **urīdu ʾīṣālan** | I’d like a receipt |
| توقف عند … | **taqif ʿinda …** | Stop at … |
| هل يمكنك تشغيل العداد؟ | **hal yumkinuka tashghīl al‑ʿaddād?** | Can you turn on the meter? |
| هل تقبل بطاقات الائتمان؟ | **hal taqbalu biṭāqāt al‑iʾtimān?** | Do you accept credit cards? |

### Negotiating the Fare (When No Meter)  

1. **Ask the fare first:** **كم الأجرة إلى الفندق؟** – “How much is the fare to the hotel?”  
2. **Agree on a price:** **حسناً، سأدفع … جنيه** – “Okay, I’ll pay … pounds.”  
3. **Confirm the route:** **هل ستأخذ الطريق السريع؟** – “Will you take the highway?”  

### Sample Taxi Conversation  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **الراكب:** إلى فندق ماريوت من فضلك. | **Al‑rākib:** ilā funduq Mārayūt min faḍlik. | To the Marriott Hotel, please. |
| **الراكب:** كم الأجرة؟ | **Al‑rākib:** kam al‑ʾujra? | How much is the fare? |
| **السائق:** ستكلفك ٢٠ جنيه. | **Al‑sāʾiq:** satakullifuka 20 junāh. | It will cost you 20 pounds. |
| **الراكب:** حسناً، أريد إيصالاً. | **Al‑rākib:** ḥasanan, urīdu ʾīṣālan. | Okay, I’d like a receipt. |
| **السائق:** تفضل. | **Al‑sāʾiq:** tafaddal. | Here you go. |

### Ride‑Sharing Apps (e.g., Uber, Careem)  

Most apps use the same Arabic interface you saw in the “Numbers” chapter for price estimates. When you confirm a ride, you’ll see:

- **الموقع** – **al‑mawqiʿ** – “Location” (pickup)  
- **الوجهة** – **al‑wajha** – “Destination”  
- **التكلفة** – **al‑taklifa** – “Cost”  

You can copy the Arabic phrase **إلى …** into the app’s destination field, and the app will handle the rest. If you need to speak to the driver, the phrases above will cover you.

---

## Putting It All Together – Mini Dialogues  

Below are three realistic scenarios that combine asking for directions, reading signs, and communicating with transport staff. Read them aloud, paying attention to the **pronunciation of emphatic consonants** (covered in the “Arabic Sounds” chapter) and the **right‑to‑left flow** of the script.

### Scenario 1: Finding a Museum on Foot  

**You:** عفواً، أين المتحف المصري؟  
**Passerby:** إذهب إلى شارع القصر، ثم انعطف يساراً عند الميدان. المتحف خلفك.  

- Vocabulary highlighted: **إذهب** (go), **شارع** (street), **انعطف يساراً** (turn left), **الميدان** (square), **خلفك** (behind you).

### Scenario 2: Taking the Bus to the Airport  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **المسافر:** أريد أن أركب باص إلى المطار. | **Al‑musāfir:** urīdu an **arkab** bāṣ ilā al‑maṭar. | I want to take a bus to the airport. |
| **المسافر:** ما هو رقم الباص؟ | **Al‑musāfir:** mā huwa raqam al‑bāṣ? | What is the bus number? |
| **الموظف:** الباص رقم ٥٠. يخرج من موقف السيارات. | **Al‑muwaẓẓaf:** al‑bāṣ raqam 50. yakhruj min mawqif al‑sayārāt. | Bus number 50. It departs from the car park. |
| **المسافر:** شكراً، إلى اللقاء! | **Al‑musāfir:** shukran, ilā al‑liqāʾ! | Thanks, goodbye! |

### Scenario 3: Hiring a Taxi to a Hotel  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **الراكب:** إلى فندق هيلتون من فضلك. | **Al‑rākib:** ilā funduq Hīltūn min faḍlik. | To the Hilton Hotel, please. |
| **الراكب:** كم الأجرة؟ | **Al‑rākib:** kam al‑ʾujra? |
| **السائق:** ٣٠ جنيه إذا أخذنا الطريق السريع. | **Al‑sāʾiq:** thalāthūn junāh ʾiḏā ʾakhadhnā al‑ṭarīq al‑sarīʿ. |
| **الراكب:** حسناً، أريد إيصالاً. | **Al‑rākib:** ḥasanan, urīdu ʾīṣālan. |
| **السائق:** تفضل. | **Al‑sāʾiq:** tafaddal. |

Practice these dialogues with a partner, swapping roles. Focus first on **accuracy of the key words** (directional verbs, place names) and then on **fluidity of the whole exchange**.

---

## Cultural Tips for Getting Around  

- **Politeness matters:** Start with **من فضلك** (please) and end with **شكراً** (thank you). Even a brief **عفواً** (excuse me) is appreciated.  
- **Eye contact and a smile** often make locals more willing to help.  
- **Ask for clarification** if a sign seems ambiguous: **ممكن توضح أكثر؟** – “Could you explain more?”  
- **When using a taxi, note the license plate** (لوحة السيارة) and keep a copy of the driver’s ID, especially at night.  
- **Public transport fares** are usually displayed on the vehicle or at the station; if not, ask **كم السعر؟** – “How much is the price?”

---

## ## Key Takeaways  

- Use **أين … ؟** and **كيف أذهب إلى … ؟** to ask for locations and directions.  
- Master the directional verbs **يمين**, **يسار**, **انعطف**, and the preposition **إلى** for giving and receiving route instructions.  
- Recognize common road‑sign words such as **ممنوع**, **سرعة**, and **موقف** to navigate streets safely.  
- Public transport vocabulary (باص, مترو, قطار, تذكرة) lets you buy tickets, ask about schedules, and understand announcements.  
- With taxi drivers, clearly state the destination (**إلى … من فضلك**), ask for the fare (**كم الأجرة؟**), and request a receipt (**أريد إيصالاً**) when needed.  
- Practice the sample dialogues to build confidence; the same structures apply across different cities and transport modes.  

By internalizing these patterns, you’ll move from a hesitant traveler to a confident navigator of Arabic‑speaking cities. Safe travels!

modules.title: Food, Dining, and Market Interactions
modules.content:
## A Bite in the Sun‑lit Café  

Imagine you’ve just arrived in Amman on a bright morning. After a short walk, you spot a bustling café with a striped awning and the aroma of freshly brewed **قهوة** drifting onto the street. You step inside, are greeted with a warm “**أهلاً وسهلاً**,” and take a seat.  

What you need now are the phrases that will let you order a drink, ask about the menu, and tell the server exactly what you want—without hesitation.

---

## Essential Food‑Related Vocabulary  

Below are the most common nouns, verbs, and adjectives you’ll encounter when dining or shopping. All words are shown in **Arabic script** with transliteration (using the Latin letters you already saw in the “Arabic Sounds” chapter) and an English gloss.

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| طعام | **ṭaʿām** | food |
| وجبة | **wajba** | meal |
| فطور | **fəṭūr** | breakfast |
| غداء | **ġadāʾ** | lunch |
| عشاء | **ʿashāʾ** | dinner |
| مشروب | **mašrūb** | drink |
| ماء | **māʾ** | water |
| شاي | **šāy** | tea |
| قهوة | **qahwa** | coffee |
| عصير | **ʿaṣīr** | juice |
| سلطة | **salāṭa** | salad |
| شاورما | **šāwirma** | shawarma |
| فلافل | **falāfil** | falafel |
| خبز | **khubz** | bread |
| لحم | **laḥm** | meat |
| خضار | **ḵuḍār** | vegetables |
| فاكهة | **fākiha** | fruit |
| سكر | **sukkar** | sugar |
| ملح | **milḥ** | salt |
| حار | **ḥār** | spicy |
| نباتي | **nabātī** | vegetarian |
| حلال | **ḥalāl** | halal |

> **Tip:** When you see a long vowel written with **Alif (ا), Waw (و),** or **Ya (ي)** in the script, pronounce it as a single, extended sound (e.g., **قهوة** = *qah**w**a*).

---

## Ordering in a Restaurant  

### 1. Getting the Waiter’s Attention  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| لو سمحت | **law samaḥt** | Please (to get attention) |
| من فضلك | **min faḍlik** | Please (polite) |

*Example:* **لو سمحت، أريد أن أطلب…** – “Please, I would like to order…”.

### 2. Stating What You Want  

Use the pattern **أريد + (noun) + (quantity if needed)**. Remember the numbers you learned in the “Numbers, Dates, and Time” chapter; they are essential for specifying amounts.

| Arabic | Transliteration | Example |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| واحد | **wāḥid** | واحد شاي – *wāḥid šāy* (one tea) |
| اثنان | **ithnān** | اثنان عصير – *ithnān ʿaṣīr* (two juices) |
| ثلاثة | **thalātha** | ثلاثة فطائر – *thalātha fuṭāʾir* (three pastries) |

*Full sentence:* **أريد ثلاثة فطائر وعصير واحد، من فضلك.** – “I would like three pastries and one juice, please.”

### 3. Asking About the Menu  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| ما هو اليوم؟ | **mā huwa al-yawm?** | What is today’s special? |
| ما هي المكونات؟ | **mā hiya al-mukawwanāt?** | What are the ingredients? |
| هل هناك خيار نباتي؟ | **hal hunāka khiyār nabātī?** | Is there a vegetarian option? |

### 4. Confirming the Order  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| هل هذا صحيح؟ | **hal hādhā ṣaḥīḥ?** | Is that correct? |
| نعم، شكراً. | **naʿam, shukran.** | Yes, thank you. |
| لا، أريد تعديل. | **lā, urīdu taʿdīl.** | No, I’d like to change it. |

---

## Expressing Dietary Preferences & Restrictions  

Travelers often need to convey allergies, religious restrictions, or personal choices. Use the following structures:

### 1. “I don’t eat …”

**أنا لا آكل …** – *anā lā ākul …*  

- **أنا لا آكل لحم** – “I don’t eat meat.”
- **أنا لا آكل أطعمة بحرية** – “I don’t eat seafood.”

### 2. “I’m allergic to …”

**أنا حساس/حساسة لـ …** – *anā ḥassās/ḥassāsa li …*  

- **أنا حساس للجلوتين** – “I’m allergic to gluten.”
- **أنا حساسة للفاستق** – “I’m allergic to pistachios.”

### 3. “Can I have it without …?”

**هل يمكن أن أحصل على … بدون …؟** – *hal yumkin an aḥṣul ʿalā … bidūn …?*  

- **هل يمكن أن أحصل على شاورما بدون صلصة حارة؟** – “Can I have shawarma without spicy sauce?”

### 4. “Is this halal?”

**هل هذا حلال؟** – *hal hādhā ḥalāl?*  

If you need a vegetarian version, add **نباتي** after the dish name: **شاورما نباتية** – “vegetarian shawarma”.

---

## Navigating the Market  

### 1. Greeting the Vendor  

Use any of the greetings you practiced earlier, e.g., **صباح الخير** (good morning) or **مساء الخير** (good evening), followed by **كيف الحال؟** – *kayfa al-ḥāl?* (How are you?).

### 2. Asking About an Item  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| ما سعر هذا؟ | **mā siʿr hādhā?** | How much is this? |
| كم الوزن؟ | **kam al-wazn?** | What is the weight? |
| هل هو طازج؟ | **hal huwa ṭāzij?** | Is it fresh? |
| هل يمكنني التجربة؟ | **hal yumkinunī al-tajriba?** | May I try it? |

### 3. Negotiating Price (Optional)  

Bargaining is common in many Arab markets. Use polite forms:

- **هل يمكن أن يكون أقل؟** – *hal yumkin an yakūn aʾqal?* (Can it be cheaper?)
- **أعطني نصف السعر إذا كان ممكناً.** – *aʿṭinī niṣf al-siʿr iḏā kāna mumkinan.* (Give me half the price if possible.)

### 4. Specifying Quantity  

Combine the number you already know with the noun:

- **واحد كيلو تفاح** – *wāḥid kīlo tufāḥ* (one kilogram of apples)
- **ثلاثة أرغفة خبز** – *thalātha arghifa khubz* (three loaves of bread)

### 5. Paying  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| أريد الفاتورة، من فضلك. | **urīdu al-fātūra, min faḍlik.** | I’d like the bill, please. |
| هل تقبل بطاقة الائتمان؟ | **hal taqbalu biṭāqat al-iʾtimān?** | Do you accept credit cards? |
| شكراً، مع السلامة. | **shukran, maʿ al-salāma.** | Thank you, goodbye. |

---

## Talking About Prices, Ingredients, and Quantities  

### 1. Numbers in Context  

Recall the cardinal numbers from the earlier chapter. When stating a price, the Arabic word **ريال** (*riyāl*) is the common currency in Saudi Arabia, **جنيه** (*junayh*) in Egypt, **دولار** (*dūlār*) elsewhere.  

**مثال:** **ثلاثة ريال** – *thalātha riyāl* (three riyals).

### 2. Describing Ingredients  

Use **مكون** (*mukawwan*) for “ingredient.” The phrase **المكونات هي …** – *al-mukawwanāt hiya …* introduces a list.

- **المكونات هي طماطم، بصل، زيت زيتون.** – “The ingredients are tomatoes, onion, olive oil.”

If you need to ask whether a dish contains a specific ingredient:

- **هل يحتوي هذا على لحم؟** – *hal yaḥtawī hādhā ʿalā laḥm?* (Does this contain meat?)

### 3. Quantity Expressions  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| قليل | **qalīl** | little |
| كثير | **kathīr** | a lot |
| نصف | **niṣf** | half |
| كامل | **kāmil** | whole |

Combine with nouns: **نصف كيلو** (*niṣf kīlo*) – “half a kilogram,” **كامل الكوب** (*kāmil al-kūb*) – “the whole cup.”

### 4. Asking for Recommendations  

- **ما هو الأفضل؟** – *mā huwa al-afḍal?* (What’s the best?)
- **هل تنصح بشيء خاص؟** – *hal tansuḥ bišayʾ khaṣṣ?* (Do you recommend anything special?)

---

## Practice Dialogues  

### Dialogue 1 – Café Order  

| Speaker | Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|--------|----------------|---------|
| **الزبون** | لو سمحت، أريد فنجان قهوة وسكّر. | **law samaḥt, urīdu finjān qahwa wa sukkar.** | Please, I’d like a cup of coffee with sugar. |
| **النادل** | هل تريد حليبًا أم سكرًا فقط؟ | **hal turīd ḥalīban am sukkaran faqaṭ?** | Do you want milk or just sugar? |
| **الزبون** | فقط سكر، من فضلك. | **faqaṭ sukkar, min faḍlik.** | Just sugar, please. |
| **النادل** | هذا هو. تفضل. | **hādhā huwa. tafaddal.** | Here it is. Enjoy. |
| **الزبون** | شكراً، بكم؟ | **shukran, bikam?** | Thank you, how much? |
| **النادل** | ثلاثة ريالات. | **thalātha riyāl.** | Three riyals. |

### Dialogue 2 – Market Purchase  

| Speaker | Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|--------|----------------|---------|
| **المشتري** | صباح الخير، كم سعر كيلو الطماطم؟ | **ṣabāḥ al-ḫayr, kam siʿr kīlo al-ṭamāṭīm?** | Good morning, how much is a kilo of tomatoes? |
| **البائع** | كيلو الطماطم بخمسة جنيه. | **kīlo al-ṭamāṭīm bi‑khamsa junayh.** | A kilo of tomatoes is five pounds. |
| **المشتري** | أريد نصف كيلو، من فضلك. | **urīdu niṣf kīlo, min faḍlik.** | I’d like half a kilo, please. |
| **البائع** | تفضّل، هل تريد شيءًا آخر؟ | **tafaddal, hal turīd shayʾan ākhir?** | Here you go, would you like anything else? |
| **المشتري** | لا، هذا كل شيء. شكراً. | **lā, hādhā kull shayʾ. shukran.** | No, that’s all. Thank you. |

---

## Cultural Tips for Food & Markets  

- **Timing:** In many Arab countries, lunch (غداء) is often taken later, around 1‑2 pm, and dinner (عشاء) can start as late as 8‑9 pm. Adjust your ordering phrases accordingly.
- **Hospitality:** It is common for hosts to offer you a drink before you even sit down. A polite **نعم، من فضلك** (yes, please) is appreciated.
- **Bargaining Etiquette:** If you choose to negotiate, do so with a smile and a **من فضلك** (please). Walking away politely after a few rounds is acceptable; the vendor may call you back with a lower price.
- **Halal Awareness:** When in doubt, ask **هل هذا حلال؟**. Most street food and market stalls adhere to halal standards, but it never hurts to confirm.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- Use **لو سمحت** or **من فضلك** to politely start a request.  
- **أريد + noun + quantity** is the core pattern for ordering food and drinks.  
- Apply the numbers you learned earlier to specify amounts, prices, and weights.  
- To convey dietary restrictions, remember **أنا لا آكل …**, **أنا حساس لـ …**, and **هل هذا حلال؟**.  
- In markets, ask **ما سعر هذا؟** and **كم الوزن؟**; combine numbers with nouns for quantity (e.g., **ثلاثة أرغفة خبز**).  
- Politeness and a friendly smile go a long way—Arabic speakers value courteous interaction as much as correct phrasing.

modules.title: Accommodation and Hospitality
modules.content:
## Arriving at the Hotel: A Quick‑Start Scenario  

You step off the taxi in front of a four‑star hotel in **القاهرة** (Al‑Qāhira, “Cairo”). The receptionist smiles and says,  

> **مرحباً!** – *Marḥabān!* – “Hello!”  

You reply, hand over your passport, and begin the check‑in process. The exchange that follows contains everything you need to get settled, ask for what you need, and handle any small hiccups that may arise.  

Below is a step‑by‑step guide that walks you through that exact moment, then expands to cover the rest of a typical stay.

---

## 1. Core Vocabulary for Lodging  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **حجز** | ḥajz | reservation |
| **غرفة** | ghurfa | room |
| **مفتاح** | miftāḥ | key |
| **جواز السفر** | jawāz al‑safar | passport |
| **بطاقة الهوية** | biṭāqat al‑huwiyya | ID card |
| **فندق** | funduq | hotel |
| **بيت ضيافة** | bayt ḍiyāfa | guesthouse |
| **مرافق** | marāfiq | facilities |
| **واي‑فاي** | wāy‑fāy | Wi‑Fi |
| **منظف** | munazzif | cleaner |
| **مناشف** | manāshif | towels |
| **مياه ساخنة** | miyāh sākhna | hot water |
| **فاتورة** | fātūra | bill / receipt |
| **نصيحة** | niṣīḥa | recommendation/tip |

> **Tip:** Most of these nouns are masculine; the plural often ends with **‑ات** (e.g., *مناشف*). When you need the definite article “the,” prepend **الـ** (al‑) as you already learned.

---

## 2. Checking In  

### 2.1 Typical Dialogue  

| English | Arabic | Transliteration |
|---------|--------|-----------------|
| **You:** Hello, I have a reservation under the name **Ahmed**. | **أهلاً، لدي حجز باسم أحمد.** | *Ahlan, ladayya ḥajz bism Ahmad.* |
| **Receptionist:** May I see your passport, please? | **من فضلك، هل يمكنني رؤية جواز السفر؟** | *Min faḍlik, hal yumkinunī ru’yat jawāz al‑safar?* |
| **You:** Here you are. | **تفضل.** | *Tafaḍḍal.* |
| **Receptionist:** How many nights will you stay? | **كم ليلة ستقضي؟** | *Kam layla sataqḍī?* |
| **You:** Three nights, from the 12th to the 15th of August. | **ثلاث ليالٍ، من 12 إلى 15 أغسطس.** | *Ṯalāth layāl, min 12 ilā 15 aghusṭus.* |
| **Receptionist:** Here is your key. Breakfast is served from 7 am to 10 am. | **هذا مفتاحك. الفطور يُقدَّم من ٧ إلى ١٠ صباحاً.** | *Hādha miftāḥak. al‑fuṭūr yuqaddam min 7 ilā 10 ṣabāḥan.* |
| **You:** Thank you. Could I have the Wi‑Fi password? | **شكراً. هل يمكنني الحصول على كلمة سر الواي‑فاي؟** | *Shukran. Hal yumkinunī al‑ḥuṣūl ʿalā kalimat sirr al‑wāy‑fāy?* |
| **Receptionist:** It is **hotel123**. | **الكلمة هي hotel123.** | *Al‑kalima hiya hotel123.* |

### 2.2 Breaking It Down  

| Phrase | When to Use | Key Words |
|--------|-------------|-----------|
| **أهلاً** / **مرحباً** | Greeting the staff. | *Ahlan / Marḥabān* |
| **لدي حجز** | Introducing your reservation. | *ladayya ḥajz* |
| **باسم …** | Giving your name. | *bism …* |
| **من فضلك** | Polite “please.” (see **Politeness** chapter) | *min faḍlik* |
| **كم ليلة** | Asking about night count. | *kam layla* |
| **من … إلى …** | Stating dates (refer to **Numbers, Dates, and Time**). | *min … ilā …* |
| **هذا مفتاحك** | Receiving the key. | *hādha miftāḥak* |
| **هل يمكنني …؟** | Polite request format. | *hal yumkinunī …?* |

> **Practice:** Swap the dates and names in the dialogue above. Record yourself saying each line, then listen for any mispronounced consonants like the emphatic **ص** (ṣ) or guttural **ع** (ʿ).

---

## 3. Requesting Room Services  

### 3.1 Common Requests  

| English Request | Arabic | Transliteration |
|-----------------|--------|-----------------|
| **Could I have an extra towel, please?** | **من فضلك، هل يمكنني الحصول على منشفة إضافية؟** | *Min faḍlik, hal yumkinunī al‑ḥuṣūl ʿalā manshafa iḍāfiya?* |
| **Is Wi‑Fi available in the room?** | **هل الواي‑فاي متوفر في الغرفة؟** | *Hal al‑wāy‑fāy mutawaffir fī al‑ghurfa?* |
| **Can you send someone to clean the room?** | **هل يمكنكم إرسال عامل تنظيف للغرفة؟** | *Hal yumkinukum irsāl ʿāmil tanẓīf lil‑ghurfa?* |
| **I need a late checkout, if possible.** | **أحتاج إلى تسجيل خروج متأخر إذا كان ذلك ممكناً.** | *Aḥtāj ilā tasjīl khurūj mutaʾakhkhir idhā kāna dhālika mumkinan.* |

### 3.2 Polite Formulas  

- **من فضلك** (*min faḍlik*) – “please.”  
- **لو سمحت** (*law samaḥt*) – “if you would be so kind.”  
- **هل …؟** (*hal …?*) – Yes‑no question.  

Combine them to soften any request:  

> **لو سمحت، هل يمكنني الحصول على مناشف إضافية؟**  
> *Law samaḥt, hal yumkinunī al‑ḥuṣūl ʿalā manāshif iḍāfiya?* – “If you please, may I have extra towels?”

---

## 4. Reporting Minor Problems Politely  

### 4.1 Typical Issues  

| Issue | Arabic Phrase | Transliteration |
|-------|---------------|-----------------|
| No hot water | **لا توجد مياه ساخنة.** | *Lā tawjadu miyāh sākhna.* |
| Air conditioner not working | **المُكيّف لا يعمل.** | *Al‑mukayyif lā yaʿmal.* |
| Light flickering | **الإضاءة تُومض.** | *Al‑iḍāʾa tūmid.* |
| TV remote missing | **الريموت مفقود.** | *Al‑rīmūt mafqūd.* |

### 4.2 Polite Complaint Structure  

1. **State the problem** clearly.  
2. **Add a polite marker** (من فضلك / لو سمحت).  
3. **Ask for a solution** using **هل يمكنكم …؟**  

**Example:**  

> **لا توجد مياه ساخنة، من فضلكم هل يمكنكم إصلاح ذلك؟**  
> *Lā tawjadu miyāh sākhna, min faḍlikum hal yumkinukum iṣlāḥ dhālika?* – “There is no hot water; please, can you fix it?”

### 4.3 Expressing Appreciation Afterwards  

After the issue is resolved, say:  

> **شكراً جزيلاً على المساعدة.** – *Shukran jazīlan ʿalā al‑musāʿada.* – “Thank you very much for the help.”

---

## 5. Getting Local Recommendations from Hotel Staff  

### 5.1 Asking for Suggestions  

| English | Arabic | Transliteration |
|---------|--------|-----------------|
| **Can you recommend a good restaurant nearby?** | **هل يمكنك أن توصي بمطعم جيد قريب؟** | *Hal yumkinuka an tusi bi‑maṭʿam jayyid qarīb?* |
| **What places should I not miss in the city?** | **ما الأماكن التي لا يجب أن أفوتها في المدينة؟** | *Mā al‑amākin allatī lā yajibu an afūṭahā fī al‑madīna?* |
| **Is there a market within walking distance?** | **هل هناك سوق على مسافة مشي؟** | *Hal hunāka sūq ʿalā masāfa mashī?* |
| **Could you arrange a taxi for me tomorrow morning?** | **هل يمكنك ترتيب تاكسي لي غداً صباحاً؟** | *Hal yumkinuka tartīb tāksī lī ghadan ṣabāḥan?* |

### 5.2 Useful Follow‑Up Phrases  

- **كم يبعد ذلك؟** – *Kam yabʿud dhālika?* – “How far is that?”  
- **هل هو مفتوح الآن؟** – *Hal huwa maftūḥ al‑ān?* – “Is it open now?”  
- **هل تحتاج إلى حجز مسبق؟** – *Hal taḥtāj ilā ḥajz musbaq?* – “Do I need a reservation?”  

---

## 6. Checking Out  

### 6.1 The Checkout Dialogue  

| English | Arabic | Transliteration |
|---------|--------|-----------------|
| **You:** I would like to check out, please. | **أريد تسجيل الخروج، من فضلك.** | *Urīd tasjīl al‑khurūj, min faḍlik.* |
| **Receptionist:** Did you enjoy your stay? | **هل استمتعت بإقامتك؟** | *Hal istamtaʿta bi‑iqāmatak?* |
| **You:** Yes, thank you. Could I have the final bill? | **نعم، شكراً. هل يمكنني الحصول على الفاتورة النهائية؟** | *Naʿam, shukran. Hal yumkinunī al‑ḥuṣūl ʿalā al‑fātūra al‑nihāʾiyya?* |
| **Receptionist:** Here it is. Would you like a receipt? | **هذه الفاتورة. هل تريد إيصالاً؟** | *Hādhihi al‑fātūra. Hal turīd īṣālan?* |
| **You:** Yes, please. And could you store my luggage for an hour? | **نعم، من فضلك. هل يمكنكم حفظ أمتعتي لساعة؟** | *Naʿam, min faḍlik. Hal yumkinukum ḥifẓ ʿaṭmāʿatī li‑sāʿa?* |
| **Receptionist:** Certainly. Here is your receipt and the key card. | **بالتأكيد. هذه إيصالك وبطاقة المفتاح.** | *Bil‑taʾkīd. Hādhihi īṣāluk wa biṭāqat al‑miftāḥ.* |

### 6.2 Key Phrases  

- **تسجيل الخروج** (*tasjīl al‑khurūj*) – check‑out.  
- **الفاتورة النهائية** (*al‑fātūra al‑nihāʾiyya*) – final bill.  
- **إيصال** (*īṣāl*) – receipt.  
- **حفظ الأمتعة** (*ḥifẓ al‑amtiʿa*) – luggage storage.  

---

## 7. Cultural Tips for Hospitality  

1. **Tipping** – While not mandatory, leaving a small tip (5–10 % of the bill) for housekeeping or bellhop is appreciated. Use the phrase **هذه إكرامية** (*hādhihi ikrāmiyya*).  
2. **Respect the “guest‑of‑honor” norm** – In many Arab hotels, the guest is treated with extra courtesy; returning a smile and a simple **شكراً** goes a long way.  
3. **Avoid direct criticism** – If a problem arises, frame it as a request for help rather than a complaint. The structure in Section 4 (problem → polite marker → solution request) follows this cultural preference.  
4. **Use the local time** – For any time‑related request (e.g., “late checkout”), be sure to specify using the 24‑hour format you learned in **Numbers, Dates, and Time** (e.g., **الساعة ١٤:٠٠** – *al‑sāʿa 14:00*).

---

## 8. Practice Exercises  

### 8.1 Fill‑in‑the‑Blank  

Complete the Arabic sentences with the appropriate word from the box.  

**Box:** *مفتاح, مناشف, واي‑فاي, فطور, فاتورة*  

1. أحتاج إلى _______ لتشغيل الغرفة.  
2. هل يمكنني الحصول على _______ إضافية؟  
3. أين _______ الصباحي يُقدم؟  
4. أريد أن أرى _______ قبل المغادرة.  
5. هل كلمة سر _______ هي **hotel123**؟

### 8.2 Role‑Play  

Partner A plays the guest; Partner B plays the receptionist. Use the checklist below, aiming for at least three exchanges per scenario.  

- **Check‑in** – Provide name, dates, and ask for Wi‑Fi password.  
- **Request** – Ask for extra towels and a cleaning service.  
- **Problem** – Report that the air conditioner is not working.  
- **Recommendation** – Ask for a nearby café that serves **قهوة** (coffee).  
- **Check‑out** – Request the final bill and luggage storage.

### 8.3 Listening Prompt (Optional)  

If you have access to a language‑learning app, search for “hotel check‑in Arabic” and listen to a native speaker. Try to write down the dialogue, then compare it with the version in Section 2.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Check‑in** uses **لدي حجز** (I have a reservation) and the polite request pattern **هل يمكنني …؟**.  
- **Room service requests** are built with **من فضلك** or **لو سمحت**, followed by the specific item (e.g., **مناشف إضافية**).  
- **Reporting problems** follows a three‑step formula: state issue → add polite marker → ask for a solution.  
- **Local recommendations** are asked with **هل يمكنك أن …؟** and can be followed by clarifying questions about distance, opening hours, or reservation needs.  
- **Check‑out** involves confirming the final bill (**الفاتورة النهائية**) and optionally arranging luggage storage.  
- **Cultural tip:** a modest tip and a friendly **شكراً** reinforce the warm hospitality typical of Arab accommodations.

modules.title: Emergency Situations and Safety
modules.content:
## When an Emergency Happens: A Traveler’s First‑Aid Toolbox  

Imagine you’ve just arrived in Marrakech. After a day of exploring the medina, you feel a sharp pain in your chest and realize you’re having trouble breathing. You need help **now**—but you don’t speak Arabic fluently. The words you choose in these critical minutes can make all the difference.  

This section equips you with the essential Arabic phrases and cultural cues you need to call for medical aid, reach the police, recover lost items, and understand common safety signs. All vocabulary is presented in three columns: **Arabic script**, **Latin transliteration**, and **English meaning**. The patterns build on the greetings and numbers you already practiced in earlier chapters, so you’ll feel comfortable using them right away.

---

## 1. Calling for Medical Help  

### 1.1 Core Phrases  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **إسعاف!** | *ʾIsʿāf!* | Ambulance! |
| **أنا بحاجة إلى طبيب** | *anā biḥājah ilā ṭabīb* | I need a doctor. |
| **أنا مريض/مريضة** | *anā marīḍ / marīḍah* | I am sick (male/female). |
| **أشعر بألم** | *ʾashʿur bi‑ʾalam* | I feel pain. |
| **أحتاج إلى مستشفى** | *ʾaḥtāj ilā mustashfā* | I need a hospital. |
| **أنا أطفح** (if you faint) | *anā aṭfaḥ* | I am fainting. |
| **ضاعف** (if you’re bleeding) | *ḍāʿif* | Bleeding. |
| **أحتاج إلى دواء** | *ʾaḥtāj ilā dawāʾ* | I need medication. |

> **Tip:** The word **إسعاف** (ʾIsʿāf) is short and unmistakable—use it even if you’re not sure what the exact problem is. Emergency responders will understand you need urgent assistance.

### 1.2 Describing Common Symptoms  

| Symptom (English) | Arabic | Transliteration |
|-------------------|--------|-----------------|
| Headache | صداع | *ṣudāʿ* |
| Fever | حرارة | *ḥarārah* |
| Nausea | غثيان | *ghathiyān* |
| Cough | سعال | *suʿāl* |
| Chest pain | ألم في الصدر | *ʾalam fī al‑ṣadr* |
| Stomach ache | ألم في البطن | *ʾalam fī al‑baṭn* |
| Dizziness | دوار | *duwār* |
| Allergic reaction | حساسية | *ḥasāsiyyah* |

**Putting it together:**  
- “I have a headache.” → *ʾindī ṣudāʿ.*  
- “My stomach hurts.” → *ʾaʿāni al‑baṭn.*  

### 1.3 Giving Your Location  

When you call an ambulance, you’ll be asked **where** you are. Use the location vocabulary you learned in the *Numbers, Dates, and Time* chapter (e.g., street numbers, landmarks).  

| Phrase | Arabic | Transliteration |
|--------|--------|-----------------|
| Near the **big market** | بالقرب من السوق الكبير | *bil‑qurb min al‑sūq al‑kabīr* |
| **In front of** the mosque | أمام المسجد | *amām al‑masjid* |
| **Next to** the hotel | بجوار الفندق | *bijiwār al‑funduq* |
| **On** (street name) | في شارع … | *fī shāriʿ …* |

**Example:**  
*ʾIsʿāf, min faḍlik! anā marīḍ wa ʾindī ʿadāʾ fī al‑sūq al‑kabīr, qarīb min al‑ḥafla.*  
“Ambulance, please! I’m sick and have a fever in the big market, near the palace.”

---

## 2. Reaching the Police or Other Emergency Services  

### 2.1 Dialing the Right Number  

Most Arab countries use **999** or **112** for emergency calls. Memorize the number for the country you’re visiting.  

| Country | Emergency number |
|---------|-------------------|
| Egypt | 122 |
| Saudi Arabia | 999 |
| United Arab Emirates | 999 |
| Jordan | 112 |
| Morocco | 190 (police), 150 (ambulance) |

When you hear the operator’s voice, start with a polite greeting (you already know **السلام عليكم** – *as‑salām ʿalaykum*).  

### 2.2 Core Police Phrases  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **شرطة!** | *shurṭa!* | Police! |
| **أنا بحاجة إلى المساعدة** | *anā biḥājah ilā al‑musāʿadah* | I need help. |
| **لقد سُرقت حقيبتي** | *laqad suriqa ḥaqībatī* | My bag was stolen. |
| **أحتاج إلى بلاغ** | *ʾaḥtāj ilā balāgh* | I need to file a report. |
| **أين أقرب مركز شرطة؟** | *ʾayna aqrab markaz shurṭa?* | Where is the nearest police station? |
| **أنا ضائع/ضائعة** | *anā ḍāiʿ / ḍāiʿah* | I am lost (male/female). |
| **الرقم هو …** | *al‑raqm huwa …* | The number is … |

### 2.3 Giving a Precise Location to Police  

Combine **directional words** you already practiced (e.g., *yamin* – right, *yasar* – left) with landmarks.  

| Phrase | Arabic | Transliteration |
|--------|--------|-----------------|
| **Turn right** | انعطف يميناً | *iʿnaṭif yamīnan* |
| **Turn left** | انعطف يساراً | *iʿnaṭif yasārān* |
| **Straight ahead** | إلى الأمام مباشرةً | *ilā al‑amām mubāsharatan* |
| **Between** (two places) | بين … و … | *bayna … wa …* |

**Sample dialogue:**  

1. **You:** *shurṭa, min faḍlik! ʾana ʿalaṭṭīl fī al‑sūq al‑kabīr wa al‑ḥafla qareeb.*  
   “Police, please! I’m lost in the big market near the palace.”

2. **Officer:** *hal yumkinuk al‑waṣf al‑mawqif?*  
   “Can you describe the location?”

3. **You:** *naḥnu fi al‑ḥadīqa, wa al‑ṭarīq yamin li‑al‑maṭar.*  
   “We are in the garden, and the road is right of the airport.”

### 2.4 Reporting a Theft or Lost Document  

| English | Arabic | Transliteration |
|---------|--------|-----------------|
| **My passport is missing** | جواز سفري مفقود | *jawāz safarī mafqūd* |
| **I lost my wallet** | فقدت محفظتي | *faqadtu maḥfaẓatī* |
| **Please write a report** | من فضلك اكتب تقريراً | *min faḍlik uktub taqrīran* |
| **I need a copy of the report** | أحتاج نسخة من التقرير | *ʾaḥtāj nuskhah min al‑taqrīr* |

**Quick phrase:** *hal yumkinuk musāʿadati? ʾindī jiwāz safarī mafqūd.* – “Can you help me? My passport is missing.”

---

## 3. Asking for Assistance with Lost Items or Documents  

### 3.1 Common Vocabulary  

| English | Arabic | Transliteration |
|---------|--------|-----------------|
| **Lost** | مفقود | *mafqūd* |
| **Found** | موجود | *mawjūd* |
| **Bag** | حقيبة | *ḥaqībah* |
| **Wallet** | محفظة | *maḥfaẓah* |
| **Key** | مفتاح | *miftāḥ* |
| **Hotel** | فندق | *funduq* |
| **Office** | مكتب | *maktab* |

### 3.2 Sample Requests  

1. **At a hotel front desk**  
   *ʾana fadiʿt maḥfaẓatī fī ghurfa al‑raʾīs. hal yumkinuk al‑tabaḥ?*  
   “I left my wallet in the main room. Can you check?”

2. **At a train station**  
   *hal raʾayt ṣandūq maḥfūẓ?* – “Did you see a locked suitcase?”

3. **To a passerby**  
   *ʾafḍal, hal raʾayt ḥaqībahī?* – “Excuse me, did you see my bag?”

### 3.3 Using Politeness Markers  

Even in urgent situations, a simple **من فضلك** (*min faḍlik* – “please”) and **شكراً** (*shukran* – “thank you”) smooth the interaction. You have already practiced these in the *Greetings, Politeness, and Small Talk* chapter.

---

## 4. Understanding Safety Signs and Warnings  

### 4.1 Common Symbols and Their Arabic Text  

| Symbol (description) | Arabic Text | Transliteration | Meaning |
|----------------------|------------|-----------------|---------|
| **No smoking** (cigarette with slash) | ممنوع التدخين | *mamnūʿ al‑tadkhīn* | No smoking |
| **Fire exit** (green rectangle with arrow) | مخارج الطوارئ | *makhārij al‑ṭawāriʾ* | Emergency exits |
| **First aid** (red cross) | الإسعافات الأولية | *al‑ʾisʿāfāt al‑ʾawwaliyyah* | First aid |
| **Danger – high voltage** (lightning bolt) | خطر – فولتية عالية | *khaṭar – fawltīyah ʿāliyah* | High voltage danger |
| **Do not enter** (person with a line) | لا تدخل | *lā tadkhul* | Do not enter |
| **Beware of dogs** (dog silhouette) | احذر من الكلاب | *iḥdhir min al‑kilāb* | Beware of dogs |
| **Closed** (door with a cross) | مغلق | *maghlūq* | Closed |

### 4.2 Reading Directions  

- **Right‑hand traffic** is standard in the Arab world; signs indicating “turn right” will show an arrow pointing **right**.  
- **Left‑hand** arrows are rarer but appear in some regions (e.g., Egypt’s older signs).  

**Key phrase when you’re unsure:** *maʿnāh?* – “What does it mean?”  

### 4.3 Quick Practice: Spot the Sign  

| Scenario | What you see | How to ask | Possible answer |
|----------|--------------|------------|-----------------|
| You see a red triangle with a skull. | خطر – مادة سامة | *maʿnāh al‑ʿalāmah?* | “It means hazardous material.” |
| A blue sign with a person swimming. | ممنوع السباحة | *hal yumkin al‑sibaḥ?* | “Swimming is not allowed.” |
| Green sign with a white “P”. | موقف سيارات | *hal hunāka maqʿad sayyārāt?* | “Is there a parking space here?” |

---

## 5. Putting the Pieces Together: Mini Dialogues  

Below are three short, realistic conversations you might encounter. Each line includes **Arabic**, **transliteration**, and **English**. Feel free to pause, repeat, and practice the rhythm.

### 5.1 Medical Emergency at a Café  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **أنت:** *ʾIsʿāf! min faḍlik, anā marīḍ wa ʾindī ʿadāʾ.* | *ʾIsʿāf! min faḍlik, anā marīḍ wa ʾindī ʿadāʾ.* | “Ambulance! Please, I’m sick and have a fever.” |
| **المُسعف:** *أين أنت الآن؟* | *ʾayna anta al‑ān?* | “Where are you now?” |
| **أنت:** *fi al‑maqha al‑qadīm, qarīb min al‑ḥafla.* | *fī al‑maqḥā al‑qadīm, qarīb min al‑ḥafla.* | “In the old café, near the palace.” |
| **المُسعف:** *سوف نأتي على الفور.* | *sawfa nāti ʿalā al‑fawr.* | “We’ll be there right away.” |

### 5.2 Reporting a Stolen Passport at the Airport  

| Arabic | Transliteration | English |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| **أنت:** *shurṭa, min faḍlik! jiwāz safarī mafqūd.* | *shurṭa, min faḍlik! jawāz safarī mafqūd.* | “Police, please! My passport is missing.” |
| **الضابط:** *هل وجدت أي دليل؟* | *hal wajadta ayyi dalīl?* | “Did you find any clue?” |
| **أنت:** *لا، لم أرى شيء.* | *lā, lam arā shayʾ.* | “No, I didn’t see anything.” |
| **الضابط:** *أين كنت آخر مرة؟* | *ʾayna kunta ʾākhar marrah?* | “Where were you last?” |
